title: Meeting Rooms II
statement:
You're given a list of `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]` is one meeting. Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that every meeting gets a room and no two meetings are in the same room at the same time.

A room becomes free the moment its meeting ends, so a meeting that ends at time `t` and another that starts at `t` can use the same room. The meetings may be given in any order, and the list may be empty (zero rooms).

Constraints: 0 to 5,000 meetings; 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000.

examples.explanation: [0, 10] and [5, 15] overlap, so two rooms are needed; [10, 20] reuses the room freed at 10.
All three meetings are running at time 3, so three rooms are needed.
Each meeting starts as the previous one ends, so one room is enough.

hints: At any moment, how many rooms are in use? How does the answer relate to the busiest moment of the day?
The count of meetings in progress only changes when a meeting starts or ends. Which of those events can raise it to a new maximum?
Process the meetings in order of start time. When one starts, can it reuse a room whose meeting has already ended? How do you know which room frees up first?
A structure that always gives you the earliest end time among the rooms in use would help. What should happen when that earliest end equals the new start?
Sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times: if the smallest end is <= the new start, replace it with the new end; otherwise push the new end. The heap size is the answer.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and where does each come from?
Can you solve it without a heap by sorting the start times and end times separately? Why does that work?
What happens to your answer if the room-reuse test uses < instead of <=?
How would you also assign each meeting a specific room number?
idealAnswerPoints: Sorts the meetings by start time
Keeps a min-heap of end times, one per room in use
Reuses the earliest-ending room when its end <= the new start, otherwise opens a new room
Answers with the heap size, equal to the largest number of simultaneous meetings
States O(n log n) time and O(n) space, and can describe the two-sorted-arrays sweep
weakAnswerSigns: Checks every pair of meetings or every time unit, which is O(n^2) or depends on the time range
Counts overlapping pairs rather than meetings in progress at once
Uses < for reuse, so back-to-back meetings need two rooms
Scans a list for the earliest end each time instead of using a heap

rubric.correctness: Correct for empty input, identical meetings, nested meetings and back-to-back chains, regardless of input order.
rubric.efficiency: O(n log n) with a heap or a two-array sweep; quadratic scans of rooms or time units are below the bar.
rubric.code_quality: Sorted input, a single heap and one reuse-or-open decision per meeting, with the equality case written deliberately.
rubric.communication: Relates rooms to the maximum overlap and explains the heap's role before coding.
